instructions: Rinse the 1 1/2 cups rice in a few changes of cold water, swishing it with your hand, until the water runs mostly clear. Drain it well.

Put the rice in a small pot with 1 3/4 cups water and bring it to a boil over high heat. Cover, turn the heat to the lowest setting and cook for 15 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave the lid on for 10 minutes. A rice cooker works too.
Meanwhile, drain the tofu. Cut each block in half lengthwise, then into slices about 1/2 inch thick. Lay them on paper towels and pat the tops dry.
Mince the 3 garlic cloves. Finely chop 3 of the scallions, and thinly slice the last one for the top.
In a bowl, stir together 6 tbsp soy sauce, 6 tbsp water, the 2 tbsp sesame oil, 2 tsp sugar, 1 tsp of the gochugaru, the garlic and the chopped scallions until the sugar dissolves.

Heat 1 tbsp of the vegetable oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium high until it shimmers. Lay in half the tofu in a single layer. Leave it for 3 to 4 minutes, until the underside is golden and the slices slide when you nudge them.
Flip each slice and cook the other side for 3 minutes, until it's golden too. Move the tofu to a plate. Add the other 1 tbsp oil and brown the rest of the tofu the same way.
Put all the tofu back in the pan. It's fine if the slices overlap a little. Turn the heat down to medium low.
Pour the sauce over the tofu and lift the edges of a few slices so it runs underneath. Simmer for 3 to 4 minutes, spooning the sauce over the top now and then.
Flip the slices and simmer the other side for 2 minutes, spooning the sauce over, until it has cooked down by about half and coats the tofu.
Take the pan off the heat. Scatter the sliced scallion and the 2 tsp sesame seeds over the top.
Taste the sauce. If it's flat, add a splash more soy sauce.
Serve over the rice, with the last 1 tsp gochugaru in a small bowl on the side.
method_notes: All three read versions pan fry firm tofu in slices until golden, then simmer it briefly in a soy sauce with sugar, gochugaru, garlic, scallion and sesame oil, spooning the sauce over as it reduces. Korean Bapsang's classic dubu jorim is the mildest, with 1 tsp gochugaru per block and water to loosen the soy. Takes Two Eggs adds mirin and covers the pan for the braise, and Korean Bapsang's spicy version skips the frying and braises the tofu in a much hotter broth over onion. This one follows the classic, doubled for a dinner with rice, and puts half the gochugaru on the side.
